This looks like a hard-to-explain trigger mismatch rather than ordinary heterogeneity.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is typically associated with interpersonal/sexual trauma or moral contamination themes. In this profile, the other appraisals are inaction guilt and distrust, and the memory items describe vivid, present-tense traumatic reliving of a terrorism event. Without any sexual assault, bodily violation, or contamination-related trigger/memory content, this appraisal is clinically discordant with the trauma type and the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: For a terrorism trauma in a 33-year-old prosecutor, the selected trigger set is weakly anchored to the trauma described. 'Needles/medical equipment' could occur if he sustained injuries, and 'alcohol smell' could occur if alcohol was present during aftermath or coping, but together they imply a medical/assault-like or hospital-associated cue pattern that is not supported anywhere else in the profile. With no memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to injury treatment, intoxication, or bodily violation, these triggers are clinically hard to place.

'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typical of sexual assault, moral contamination, or exposure involving bodily fluids. In a terrorism case it is not impossible, but here it is not supported by the rest of the selected items: the memories emphasize disorganization and nowness, and the appraisals emphasize guilt and distrust, not bodily violation or pollution. This makes the contamination item the least coherent appraisal in the set.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For an adult male prosecutor with terrorism trauma, the appraisal of feeling 'dirty or contaminated' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other items center on sensory trauma triggers (alcohol smell, explosion sounds), disorganized yet vivid reliving memory, and guilt/distrust appraisals, which fit terrorism exposure. 'Contamination' more strongly suggests trauma involving sexual assault, bodily violation, or moral taint, and here it lacks support from the memory, trigger, or strategy nodes. This makes it a clinically questionable outlier within the allowed components.

vignette: David, a 33-year-old prosecutor from North America, has been grappling with symptoms following a traumatic experience of terrorism. His life took an unexpected turn when he was caught in the aftermath of a bombing that left several people injured and others dead. The event remains vividly etched in his memory, making it difficult for him to distinguish between what happened then and what is happening now. David often feels very tired or exhausted, which he attributes to the mental toll of reliving the trauma repeatedly. This fatigue serves as a trigger that heightens his emotional distress. He recalls the sound of an explosion one day while attending a professional conference, and it instantly transported him back to the scene of the bombing. The memory was so vivid and real that he felt like he was reliving the moment all over again. The trauma has left David with fragmented memories. When he tries to recount what happened during the attack, his mind goes blank or jumps between disconnected scenes. Despite this, the images in his mind are incredibly detailed and feel more real than memories of ordinary events. He often finds himself feeling as though the bombing is happening right now rather than something that occurred in the past. David’s inability to form a coherent narrative of what happened has led him to believe he will never forgive himself for not doing enough to prevent the tragedy. This belief is reinforced by his fragmented and vivid memories, which replay the events over and over again, each time with a different emphasis on his perceived failures. The more real these memories feel, the more David questions whether he could have acted differently or protected others. His feelings of guilt and inaction are compounded by a growing sense of distrust towards others. He feels that people are not what they seem, and this suspicion is only exacerbated when triggered by certain olfactory cues like the smell of alcohol, which reminds him of the chaos and confusion during the bombing. Every time he encounters these triggers, his negative appraisals intensify, making it increasingly difficult for him to trust those around him. David’s marriage has also been affected as a result of these symptoms. His wife has noticed changes in his behavior, such as increased irritability and withdrawal from social activities. He feels he is failing her by not being able to fully engage with everyday life or protect her the way he believes he should have protected others during the attack. The combination of guilt, distrust, and vivid memories keeps David trapped in a cycle where each component reinforces the other. His fragmented memories fuel his negative appraisals, which in turn make him more susceptible to triggers that heighten these emotions. He feels stuck and unable to break free from this cycle. David finally sought help after realizing how deeply his trauma was affecting his ability to perform at work and maintain a fulfilling relationship with his wife. What frightened him most was the possibility of being defined by this event, trapped in an endless loop of guilt and fear. He is hoping for relief from these symptoms so he can regain control over his life and reconnect with the world around him.
